questions.text: The lesson highlights three GDPR principles as especially relevant when a school considers AI tools. Which are they?

options.text: Purpose limitation — data collected for one purpose may not be used for an unrelated one without a lawful basis
Data minimisation — only the data strictly necessary for a given purpose should be processed
Storage limitation — personal data should not be kept longer than necessary
Risk classification — every AI system must be assigned to a risk tier before a school may use it
Continuous disclosure — parents must be notified on each occasion an AI tool is used in a lesson

questions.explanation: Purpose limitation, data minimisation and storage limitation are the three principles the lesson singles out. Risk classification belongs to the EU AI Act, which the lesson presents as a second layer, and disclosure is a component of the school's own policy rather than a GDPR principle.

questions.text: A teacher wants to use a general-purpose AI assistant to prepare differentiated materials. What is the lesson's default position?

options.text: Appropriate for teacher preparation using anonymised or non-personal material, and not appropriate for processing identifiable student data.
Appropriate for any school purpose, because the teacher rather than the provider decides how the output is used.
Never appropriate in a school, because these tools are built by companies outside the school's control.
Appropriate for identifiable student data as well, provided the teacher deletes the conversation afterwards.

questions.explanation: The lesson's default is that general-purpose assistants serve teacher preparation on anonymised material. Sending identifiable student data to an external provider is a transfer to an external processor, requiring a lawful basis, appropriate safeguards and in many cases a signed Data Processing Agreement.

questions.text: Because schools use AI systems rather than build them, the EU AI Act's obligations for high-risk uses do not apply to schools.
questions.explanation: The lesson states that these obligations apply even to schools that develop no AI systems themselves but use them in contexts classified as high-risk, such as admissions, grading high-stakes examinations, or detecting academic dishonesty.

questions.text: What does the lesson recommend as the default for lower secondary students?

options.text: Supervised use within specific lessons, with clear pedagogical objectives and no entry of personal data.
Structured individual use for preparation, practice and metacognitive reflection.
The same position as for primary students: no direct use of general-purpose tools.
Unrestricted individual use, provided the school has approved the tool.

questions.explanation: The lesson calibrates student use to developmental stage — restricted at primary level, supervised within lessons at lower secondary, structured individual use at upper secondary — and adds that direct individual use outside supervised contexts is typically not appropriate at the lower secondary level.
